market_context: United States; home handling of commercially washed refrigerated shell eggs
title: Should you wash eggs before storing them?

seo.title: Should you wash eggs before storing them?
seo.meta_description: No. Store-bought U.S. eggs are already washed and sanitized commercially. Washing them again at home can increase contamination risk and is unnecessary.
seo.search_intent: Find out whether store-bought eggs should be washed before refrigeration and why commercial washing is different from washing eggs at home.

excerpt: No. USDA says consumers should not wash commercially packaged eggs before storing or using them. U.S. graded eggs have already been washed and sanitized under controlled processing conditions and are kept refrigerated. Rewashing at home is unnecessary and can increase contamination risk if wash water is drawn through shell pores or extra handling cracks the shell.
content_html:
U.S. supermarket eggs may look as though another rinse would make them cleaner before they go into the refrigerator. It does not improve their safety: USDA specifically advises consumers not to wash commercially packaged eggs at home.

Store-bought U.S. eggs have already been washed

USDA-graded eggs are washed and sanitized by processors under controlled conditions using compounds permitted for food processing. The process controls water temperature so contaminated wash water is not drawn into the egg through pores in the shell.

Commercial washing removes the natural outer coating, often called the bloom or cuticle. USDA explains that processors commonly replace some protection with a light coating of edible mineral oil. The eggs then move through a refrigerated system.

Why washing them again can backfire

An eggshell is porous. If home wash water is cooler than the egg or otherwise creates unfavorable pressure conditions, water at the surface can be drawn inward. If the water or shell carries microorganisms, that is the opposite of what the wash was meant to accomplish.

Extra handling also creates more opportunities to crack a shell or spread contamination to hands, the faucet and the sink. A visually cleaner egg is not automatically a microbiologically safer egg.

What to do when you bring eggs home

USDA recommends putting eggs promptly in a refrigerator at 40 °F or below, keeping them in their original carton and storing them in the main body of the refrigerator rather than the door.

The carton protects against breakage, reduces odor pickup and keeps package dates and handling information with the eggs. The refrigerator door experiences greater temperature swings every time it is opened.

What if an egg looks dirty?

USDA recommends buying Grade A or AA eggs with clean, uncracked shells. If a commercial egg is unusually dirty or cracked, washing it at home is not the way to restore normal safety.

A cracked egg should not be purchased. If a shell cracks accidentally after purchase, handling depends on when and how the crack occurred; an egg of uncertain history should be discarded rather than rinsed and put back into long storage.

Should you wash it right before cracking?

USDA says washing commercially packaged eggs is unnecessary before use as well as before storage. Instead, focus hygiene on what actually becomes contaminated during preparation: wash hands, utensils, equipment and work surfaces with hot soapy water before and after contact with raw egg.

Crack eggs cleanly and avoid using the shell itself to move yolks back and forth when a recipe does not require it, because that creates more contact between the edible contents and the shell exterior.

Why advice looks different in Europe

European retail practice is not identical. EU Class A eggs are normally sold without industrial washing so their natural cuticle remains intact, whereas U.S. commercial eggs are washed before sale and then kept refrigerated.

Despite the different processing systems, the consumer takeaway converges: neither system treats casual home washing before storage as a useful safety step.

The practical rule

Put U.S. store-bought eggs in the refrigerator, not under the faucet. They have already been commercially washed. Keep them cold at 40 °F or below, in the carton, and put your cleaning effort into hands and kitchen surfaces after handling raw egg.

faq.question: Should I wash supermarket eggs before refrigerating them?
faq.answer: No. USDA says it is unnecessary and not recommended because commercially packaged eggs have already been washed and sanitized under controlled conditions.

faq.question: Can washing eggs push bacteria inside?
faq.answer: It can increase that risk. USDA explains that wash water can be drawn through shell pores under unfavorable conditions, which is one reason home rewashing is discouraged.

faq.question: Where should eggs be stored in the refrigerator?
faq.answer: USDA recommends the original carton in the main part of a refrigerator at 40 °F or below, rather than the door.

faq.question: Why aren't European supermarket eggs washed the same way?
faq.answer: EU Class A eggs are normally not industrially washed so the natural cuticle remains intact. The U.S. uses controlled commercial washing followed by refrigerated distribution.
